prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms opened the 10^-18 regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I move from B050 to B051 as a single-part prize, and I want to be clear that the reason is the credit question and not a change in my view of the physics. After the first round, six members hold the same two names for the clocks, and nobody has disputed that independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) agree at the 10^-18 level. That is the reproducibility standard I apply to theory and experiment alike. Lindroth and Kroll have given the answer to the overlap objection that I could not give from my own field: the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and the control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock rests on a different idea, a trap whose light shift cancels between the clock states, so that many atoms are interrogated at once. If the citation is written around that step, the prize is distinct and honest about its lineage. Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking it to record accuracy and the many-body regime is a compact two-name configuration. B050 remains the candidate that excites me most as a condensed-matter physicist, a genuinely new state of electronic matter that theory told us where to look for, but I cannot show the committee a three-name credit for it that survives scrutiny.
statement.case_against: The objections to B051 are real. It follows two recent prizes in precision measurement, so it is easier to call it an incremental step than a new state of matter, which is the point I made to Kroll and still hold as a matter of taste. The SI second has not been redefined, so some of the impact is prospective. Ye's credit could be read as refinement and records, as Olsson says, rather than invention, and Lemonde and others around 2001-2003 may have a priority claim that I cannot settle from memory. A B050 prize would also be a stronger scientific statement about condensed matter, and by moving away from it I accept that the committee's prize may be less surprising. The B050 plus B051 combination that the chair asked about is not available to me: Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori and Ye are five people, over the three-person limit, so I have to choose.

responses.point: Olsson says the HgTe route was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, that Zhang's death means the gap cannot be closed, and that with a clean two-name configuration available she would not choose the contested attribution first.
responses.response: In round 1 I argued that Kane and Mele supplied the invariant and the model and that Molenkamp's experiment is the decisive test. I still think that chain is scientifically accurate, but your argument is about what the committee can defend in a citation, not about the chain, and on that I now agree. Three members have made the same point independently and none of us can say what the 3D contributors would be owed under a three-name limit. I accept your ordering and have moved to B051. I join you in asking for the 2001-2003 priority papers to be checked, since the same standard has to apply to Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Danielsson says Kane-Mele-Molenkamp skips the idea that Molenkamp tested, that the 2016 prize overlaps more than I allowed, and that B050 should be a first alternative rather than the lead; he would drop B009 and fall back to B050 if Halzen's credit cannot be defended.
responses.response: You were right on attribution and I now follow you in moving B050 down to an alternative. On the 2016 overlap I still disagree: Z2 topology protected by spin-orbit coupling without a magnetic field is a distinct physical idea from the quantum Hall and Kosterlitz-Thouless work that was recognised then. But I do not need that point to settle the matter, since the credit gap alone is enough. I also share your caution on B009. Since a two-part prize with B051 would be three people, I understand why it appeals, but I cannot judge the astroparticle credit and I would not support a one-person IceCube award unless the expert reports resolve who the community regards as decisive.

responses.point: Lindroth treats the lattice clock as a distinct achievement resting on the magic-wavelength idea, says its independent reproduction settles maturity, and would not wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: This answered the question I put to you in round 1 about whether the BHZ gap or the novelty of the clock decides the ranking. Your point that the 2012 prize concerned single ions, which give a stable clock but with a low count rate, while the lattice clock interrogates many atoms at once, is the physical difference that I could not supply. I agree that the prize should not wait for the SI decision, because the independent confirmation is already in hand. I would ask only that the citation say lattice and magic wavelength explicitly, so the reader sees the distinction from the comb and ion prizes, and I support your wish that Ye's many-body clock work be described carefully.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the condensed-matter members, who are outside AMO, think the impact of the lattice clock beyond atomic physics is really as broad as claimed, and asks to be told if Kane and Mele's Z2 classification stands alone as the decisive step.
responses.response: As the condensed-matter voice you asked for, I think the breadth claim holds up on one criterion that matters to me: clock-to-clock comparisons across continents are reproducible measurements at a level where systematic effects such as the many-body spin-exchange shifts can be tested against theory, and that is also where first-principles many-body theory contacts the experiment. On your other question, I cannot say that the Z2 classification stands alone as the decisive step, because the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested came from other people, so that is a reason I stepped back from B050. On the cost, I note your remark that Ye overlaps with the cold-molecule candidate, but that does not trouble me for this prize.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B050 as his first alternative, would not oppose a topological prize if the credit can be settled, but thinks it is not settled today, and says the clock citation should be written around simultaneous interrogation of many atoms at the magic wavelength.
responses.response: I agree with both parts. On B050 the credit is not settled and I do not think that an outside report can add names to a three-person limit, so I am no longer proposing it as the lead. On the citation, I have used the magic-wavelength and many-atom wording you and Lindroth recommend. Where I differ is on the two-part pairing with B009. A thematic pairing of unrelated physics is something I would accept only if both parts stood on their own, and the credit problem in IceCube means that I cannot be sure of that.

uncertainties: Whether the 2001-2003 priority record supports exactly Katori and Ye, or whether Lemonde or others should replace or join Ye, which I take from memory and would want an outside expert to check.
Whether Ye's credit rests on the invention or on accuracy and many-body records, and how to word that in the citation.
Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the SI redefinition should delay the award.

Whether a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize could become defensible if an outside report finds that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's contribution is secondary to the Z2 classification; that would bring me back to B050.
statement.conflict_note: My earlier disclosure stands. I have no recorded connection to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. My electronic-structure work is close in field to B050 and B002 but that is not a personal tie, and I note that I am now moving away from the field closest to mine, which should reduce any sympathy bias. Johansson has disclosed a stake in B038 and should step back from that item. I have no tie that requires recusal on B051.
